Detailed PMRL notes:
Problem: Standard model-based reinforcement learning factors decision-making into two stages: learning is used only to approximate an unknown dynamics model (a supervised learning problem), and the rest of the work is offloaded to a classical trajectory optimizer (e.g., iLQG/MPC-style routines as in Tassa et al. 2012, Posa et al. 2014, Kelly 2017). The paper argues this composition is empirically brittle: powerful trajectory optimizers aggressively exploit inaccuracies in the learned model, so the resulting plans often resemble adversarial examples rather than feasible, near-optimal trajectories (Talvitie 2014; Ke et al. 2018). The difficulty is not purely a modeling issue either - MPPI driven by ground-truth dynamics performs poorly on long-horizon sparse-reward control, and model-free offline RL algorithms struggle with credit assignment when reaching a goal requires hundreds of steps.

A second bottleneck concerns flexibility. Offline model-free agents such as IQL perform well mainly in the single-goal setting they were trained for and degrade substantially when the goal location is randomized (multi-task), and prior methods like BCQ and CQL score near zero on conditional task variants such as stacking blocks in a specified order or matching novel rearrangements - i.e., they cannot adapt to new test-time goal configurations without retraining. The paper therefore asks what it would look like to fold as much of the trajectory-optimization pipeline as possible into the modeling problem itself, such that sampling from the model and planning with it become nearly identical.
Method: Diffuser is a diffusion probabilistic model defined directly over state-action trajectories. A forward diffusion process q(tau^i | tau^{i-1}) progressively corrupts a complete trajectory with noise, and a learned reverse denoising model p_theta(tau^{i-1} | tau^i) - implemented as a temporal U-Net that treats the (state, action) sequence like an image across time - is trained to undo one corruption step at a time. Planning then becomes ancestral sampling from the reverse process: starting from pure noise, the model iteratively refines it into a coherent trajectory. In this formulation, 'sampling from the model' and 'planning with the model' are nearly the same operation, eliminating the separation between model estimation and an external optimizer.

Two standard generative-modeling tools are reinterpreted as coherent planning strategies. First, classifier-guided sampling: gradients of a learned value/reward signal steer reverse-diffusion samples toward high-return regions, replacing the explicit cost minimization of a trajectory optimizer with reward-guided denoising. Second, inpainting: a subset of trajectory elements (e.g., the start state and goal state) is clamped to specified values at every denoising step while the model 'inpaints' the remaining states and actions, yielding test-time goal conditioning ('planning as inpainting'). Because conditioning happens at sampling time, a single trained model serves as a multi-task planner - changing the goal only requires changing the conditioning - and the same mechanism supports flexible test-time specifications such as desired block-stacking orders or rearrangements.
Result: On long-horizon multi-task planning in Maze2D (D4RL; reward of 1 only at the goal location, episodes spanning hundreds of steps), Diffuser plans by inpainting a fixed start and goal state and executes the sampled trajectory as an open-loop plan. It achieves scores above 100 in all three maze sizes (U-Maze, Medium, Large), outperforming a reference expert policy and the best model-free offline RL baselines (IQL being the strongest), while MPPI with ground-truth dynamics performs poorly - showing long-horizon planning is hard even without prediction error. In the multi-task variant (Multi2D) where the goal is randomized each episode, Diffuser performs as well as in the single-task setting with no retraining (only the conditioning goal changes), whereas the best model-free method, IQL with hindsight experience relabeling (Andrychowicz et al., 2017), suffers a substantial performance drop.

For test-time flexibility, all methods were trained on 10,000 demonstration trajectories generated by PDDLStream for block stacking (sparse reward of 1 upon successful stack placements). Diffuser obtains 58.7 +/- 2.5 on Unconditional Stacking, 45.6 +/- 3.1 on Conditional Stacking (specified block order), and 58.9 +/- 3.4 on Rearrangement (matching reference blocks in a novel arrangement), for an average of 54.4. In contrast, CQL achieves only 24.4 on Unconditional Stacking and 0.0 on both conditional tasks (average 8.1), and BCQ scores 0.0 on all tasks (average 0.0). Diffuser thus generalizes to goal configurations unseen during training where model-free baselines fail entirely. The paper also studies practical runtime considerations, identifying effective ways to speed up the diffusion sampling procedure while suffering minimal performance degradation.
Limitation: The most explicit documented constraint is computational: iterative denoising makes planning expensive at decision time, and the authors devote analysis to 'practical runtime considerations of diffusion-based planning,' studying the most effective ways to speed up planning (e.g., reducing the number of denoising steps) while suffering minimal performance loss - indicating an inherent compute-versus-quality trade-off. In the Maze2D evaluation the sampled trajectory is used purely as an open-loop plan, so robustness to compounding errors under closed-loop, receding-horizon execution is not exercised in these results. Planning quality further depends on the learned guidance signal (value/reward model) that steers denoising, and flexible task specification relies on casting goals or constraints as trajectory elements that can be inpainted, which may not capture arbitrary constraint types. Finally, the heterogeneous-data recovery capability is demonstrated on the studied control suites, leaving broader domain generalization untested in the presented results.

While conceptually simple, this combination has a number of empirical shortcomings, suggesting that learned models may not be well-suited to standard trajectory optimization. In this paper, we consider what it would look like to fold as much of the trajectory optimization pipeline as possible into the modeling problem, such that sampling from the model and planning with it become nearly identical. The focus of our experiments is to evaluate Diffuser on the capabilities we would like from a data-driven planner. In particular, we evaluate (1) the ability to plan over long horizons without manual reward shaping, (2) the ability to generalize to new conﬁgurations of goals unseen during training, and (3) the ability to recover an effective controller from heterogeneous data of varying quality. We conclude by studying practical runtime considerations of diffusion-based planning, including the most effective ways of speeding up the planning procedure while suffering minimally in terms of performance. 5.1 Long Horizon Multi-Task Planning We evaluate long-horizon planning in the Maze2D environments (Fu et al., 2020), which require traversing to a goal location where a reward of 1 is given. No reward shaping is provided at any other location. Because it can take hundreds of steps to reach the goal location, even the best model-free algorithms struggle to adequately perform credit assignment and reliably reach the goal (Table 1). We plan with Diffuser using the inpainting strategy to condition on a start and goal location. (The goal location is also available to the model-free methods; it is identiﬁable by being the only state in the dataset with non-zero reward.) We then use the sampled trajectory as an open-loop plan. Diffuser achieves scores over 100 in all maze sizes, indicating that it outperforms a reference expert policy.
